description: More than 400,000 specialists helped make the Moon landing one of humanity’s greatest breakthroughs. Now it is your turn to make an impact! Whether you are a web developer new to astronomy and data analysis, or the reverse, join us in building a public-facing tool that displays images of the sky from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. You do not need to know everything; bring your unique perspective, learn with the team, and take on the challenge!
summary:
Somewhere past Neptune, there could be an undiscovered planet moving through our solar system, but nobody knows exactly where to look. In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto by blinking between photographs of the same part of the sky, and almost a hundred years later we asked if that same technique could help investigate Planet X using NASA’s infrared observations. That question became SkyFlip.

SkyFlip takes real NASA SPHEREx observations and turns them into an interactive tool where users can compare images from different dates, find moving objects, explore full resolution detector frames, and look at individual sources right in their browser. We went past just showing images by adding WCS based alignment, Gaia reference star overlays, alignment verification, an interactive time machine, and a calculator that turns observed motion into tangential velocity, and we built it around five real astronomical targets to show how small movements in space can be investigated with actual infrared data.

We haven’t discovered Planet X. We built a tool that lets anyone investigate the kind of motion that could help reveal it.
details:
What if the next big discovery in astronomy was already hiding in NASA’s data? SkyFlip is an interactive tool that brings Clyde Tombaugh’s blink comparison technique into the modern day. In 1930, Tombaugh discovered Pluto by switching between photographs of the same part of the sky and spotting a point of light that had moved. SkyFlip does the same thing with real infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission, which lets users see how objects in space move between observations taken on different dates.

Users can pick a target, compare observations with a blink comparator, move through time, look at full resolution detector images, and check out individual sources. Instead of just showing finished astronomy pictures, SkyFlip gives people the tools to explore the actual observations, which is what makes it different.

To do this, we get SPHEREx Level 2 IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, and ZODI products from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive. We use World Coordinate System (WCS) information to line up the observations from different dates, so the same part of the sky can be compared accurately. We also built tiled image pyramids with 256 pixel float32 tiles, which lets the full 2040 by 2040 detector frames be explored right in a browser. Other features are Gaia reference star overlays, alignment verification, an interactive time machine, and a tangential velocity calculator.

For our tech stack, we used Python, FastAPI, Astropy, and reproject for the backend, and Vite, React, and TypeScript for the frontend.

Throughout development we thought about scientific accuracy, image alignment, data accessibility, browser performance, and how easy it is to use. Motion in space can be really small, so accurate alignment and reliable reference information are very important. For example, WISE 0855 has a proper motion of about eight arcseconds per year, which across observations 372 days apart works out to roughly 1.3 pixels at SPHEREx’s detector scale.

What makes SkyFlip creative is that it combines a technique from almost a hundred years ago with modern infrared survey data. Instead of recreating the discovery of Pluto with simulated photographs, we built an interactive platform around real NASA observations.

Our goal is to make exploring astronomy easier for students, researchers, astronomy fans, and the public. SkyFlip does not claim to have discovered Planet X. It gives people a way to look at real observations, notice small motions in space, and take part in how scientific exploration actually works.
